chapters.title: 2 Notation of Notes, Clefs, and Ledger Lines

media.alt: A picture of elliptical noteheads, some filled in as solid black and one left open. Vertical stems, horizonal beams, and curved flags are also depicted.
Five horizontal lines spaced evenly.
Provides an illustration of correct noteheads, both open (white) and filled in (black). The noteheads are drawn on both lines and spaces.

Shows incorrect examples of noteheads. Some of the noteheads are too small, some are too big, and some are the wrong shapes. Noteheads on both lines and spaces are depicted, and there are both open and filled in noteheads.
Notes with stems are shown. Above the middle line, their stem points down, on the left side of the note. Below the middle note, their stem points up, on the right side of the note.
Three seconds are shown. The lower note is always on the left.
Three incorrect seconds are shown. One stacks two notes directly on top of each other. The right note is on the bottom in the other two pairs of notes.
Four notes (C4) are placed after four different clefs: a treble, bass, alto, and tenor clef.
A treble clef is drawn in three steps.
A bass clef is drawn in three steps.
An alto clef is drawn in four steps.
A tenor clef is drawn in four steps.
A hand-drawn alto and tenor clef, in which the clefs are shaped like the letter K.
Depicts a staff with a bass clef. Above and below the staff are ledger lines. No noteheads are present.
A treble clef is on the left side of a staff. Notes (with beams and stems) are placed above and below the staff, on ledger lines.
To the left, a picture of correctly drawn ledger lines and notes is shown. To the right, incorrectly drawn ledger lines are shown. There should be no extra ledger line above or below notes.
A treble clef is on the left of a staff. The letter names of the lines are labeled. Bottom to top these are: E, G, B, D, and F.
A treble clef is to the left of a staff. The letter names of the spaces are labeled. From bottom to top these are: F, A, C, and E.
A staff with a bass clef to its left. The letter names of the lines are labeled. Bottom to top these are: G, B, D, F, A.
A staff with a bass clef to the left. The letter names of the spaces are labeled. They are (bottom to top): A, C, E, and G.
A staff with an alto clef to the left. The lines are labeled with letter names. These are (bottom to top): F, A, C, E, and G.
A staff with an alto clef on the left side. The letter names of the spaces are labeled. These are (bottom to top): G, B, D, F.
A staff with a tenor clef to the left. Letter names for the lines are labeled. These are (bottom to top): D, F, A, C, E.
A staff with a tenor clef to the left. The spaces are labeled. These are (bottom to top): E, G, B, D.
A staff with a treble clef. Ledger lines are used to extend the staff, with the letter names G, A, B, and C.
A staff with a bass clef. Ledger lines extend the staff down with the letter names F, E, D, and C.

chapters.title: 5 Half Steps, Whole Steps, and Accidentals

media.alt: A piano keyboard is shown with the white keys labeled. Half steps between B/C, E/F, G and G sharp and A and A flat are shown.
A piano keyboard is shown and white keys are labeled. Whole steps between A and B, E and F sharp, and D flat and E flat show also labeled.

Correct and incorrect ways of drawing accidentals are shown. The correct accidentals appear to the left of a note, on the same line or space as the note. Incorrect accidentals are too large, too small, or are on a different line or space than the note.
A piano keyboard is shown. The white and black keys are labeled. Each black key note has both a sharp and a flat name.
A piano keyboard is shown with white and black keys labeled. Additionally, double accidentals are shown on some of the white keys.
Nine different octaves are shown in the treble and bass clefs, each beginning and ending with the pitch "C." They are labeled with their ASPN label; C0, C1, C2, etc.
The notes C, D, E, F, G, A, and B in a treble clef
A piano keyboard with each octave labeled by number. The first two white keys are the "0" octave; each new octave (octave 1, octave 2, octave 3, etc.) starts at the note "C."
Eight dynamics are arranged from softest to loudest.
A crescendo is shown to the left, and a decrescendo is shown on the right.
A timeline shows the Medieval, Renaissance, Baroque, Classical, Romantic, and Post-Tonal periods
